title: Baywater Animal Rescue needs foster placements
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Baywater Animal Rescue needs foster placements

 June 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 346
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Ahead of an expected influx of animals in the coming months, Baywater Animal Rescue is on a mission to find the shelter's residents forever homes.Historically, summer is the busiest season for animal rescue organizations due to an increase in kitten and puppy litters, a rise in lost and stray animals as outdoor activity increases, and a decline in volunteers.
But even as demand increases, Baywater Animal Rescue manages to shelter as many animals as possible. "We will never move an animal out of our facility through euthanasia to make room for another," said Executive Director Steffanie Malkus.
Malkus and her staff have made the facility as much of a home as possible for the animals residing there. The cats and kittens have their own space with three rooms, cat trees galore and a "catio" so the more adventurous felines can roam inside and outside.
The dogs and puppies have the other side of the facility, where they have individual kennels, multiple outdoor play areas with balls and agility courses, and once it's hot enough, kiddie pools to cool off.
Fostering is near and dear to Malkus, who is a self-proclaimed foster failure. "The first night we brought them home, we all piled on the couch, and it was just one big love fest from then on out," she said. Four years later, she couldn't imagine life without her rescue cat Sydney and dog Lucas.
Baywater makes fostering easy. Staff sends their animals to their foster homes with all the necessities and helps train foster volunteers who are new to pets.
"There are certain requirements as to what your knowledge is with caring for an animal or your willingness to be taught on certain care for animals," said former Executive Director Carly Stockus. "There's always different types of fosters that are needed," she said.
Baywater Animal Rescue also encourages community members to come by and volunteer. "If you're not quite ready to foster, you can always come down and volunteer and get to know some of the animals," Malkus said.
Volunteers of all ages are welcomed. Minors must be with a guardian.

author: Staff Writer
content:

 June 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 78
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Shrek, left, and Donkey arrived at the Talbot Humane Society after what looked like an unapproved swamp adventure. They were filthy, stinky and clearly living the outdoor kennel life. No manners. No training. No clue. They may still be working on basic commands and getting accustomed to the pet lifestyle, but Shrek and Donkey are loving, hard working dogs who are ready to be part of someone's family. title: Thanks for 1,000 American flags
author: Staff Writer
content:
Thanks for 1,000 American flags

 June 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 292
 Words 

 Read News Document

 American flags decorate Easton and other area locations this Memorial Day weekend.It started in 2012 with the idea of placing a few American flags around our community during the Memorial Day weekend. This year over 1,000 American flags were displayed in 14 different locations.
Did you ever wonder who did it and why?
The Rotary Club of Easton started what has become a tradition not only in our small town but to other Rotary Clubs across the Delmarva area and in many other states. Those flags represent the visual part of our annual Flags for Heroes program. It was meant to help all of us remember what Memorial Day was really all about.
Businesses, families and individuals sponsor every one of those flags to honor the heroes whether they have fallen in battle, veterans, first responder, etc. Because of the overwhelming support we have received, our club has used those funds locally by supporting deserving community organizations such as, Talbot Hospice, For All Seasons, the Talbot Paramedics Foundation, the Talbot Sheriff's Office, Easton and all area volunteer fire departments, Easton Police Department, local cemeteries that are the final resting place for veterans and many other amazing initiatives.
This would not have been possible if it wasn't for the Town of Easton and the Talbot County Council which allows us to display the flags throughout the area. We must also recognize the Easton Utilities for all their support, The Star Democrat and our local radio stations (WCEI and WINK). Lastly to the wonderful people and businesses of our community, who contribute so generously.
The Rotary Club of Easton would like to say thank you. Memorial Day reminds us of those who gave the ultimate sacrifice for freedom.
To learn more go to: flagsforheroes.org.
JOHN FLOHR
JACKIE WILSON
Rotary Club of Easton

title: Welcome to the Star Democrat's new newsletter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Welcome to the Star Democrat's new newsletter

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Headlines 
 
 202
 Words 

 Read News Document

 If you've been reading our newsletters for a while, you've probably noticed that this one looks a little different.We are excited to share our new newsletter, a revamped way to connect with our readers. Five days a week, our newsletter will deliver the most relevant news directly to your inbox. The headlines will be curated to ensure you see what stories matter the most in our community.
This new format gives us an opportunity to offer you a glimpse into our newsroom and introduce you to the people who put together your community news.
The Mid-Shore community is tight-knit, bound together by mutual interests in the area's heritage, culture and potential. We also find topics we are divided on — growth and development, traffic, the best place in town to get a crab cake. And we know that what you value most is transparency and being well informed.
This will be your direct connection to our common interest, Mid-Shore readers, and we hope that by directly talking with our readers, we can continue to foster the strong community bonds we've been forging for more than two centuries.
From the bottom of our hearts, thank you for your sincere interest in supporting local news.
— Wendy Weitzel 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

The Hobby Fair was started in 1930 as a school project and exhibit initiated by Federalsburg High School Industrial Arts teacher, Max Chambers. It was then held yearly through the 1930s as a community event but was discontinued for many, many years. The tradition was revived by the Historical Society in 2002 and has become an annual showcase. 443-786-4086 for details.

Samaritan House Thrift Shop, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Wednesday to Friday; 9 a.m. to noon Saturday. 5th Street behind the post office.
Third Thursdays in Downtown Denton, 5 to 7 p.m., third Thursdays, downtown. Businesses extend their hours and offer specials. Info: DowntownDenton.com.
Aaron's Place Food Pantry, 9:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., Tuesday & Wednesday, 401 Aldersgate Drive.
Paws for Reading, 3:40 to 4:25 p.m., every fourth Thursday, Central Branch library. Children ages 5 to 12 can proactice reading to a trained service dog. One registrant per session. Register: carolib.libcal.com.
Museum of Rural Life, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., every Saturday, 16 N. Second Street. World War I and II, a sharecropper's cabin, new Buffalo Soldier exhibit, among many other artifacts and stories about Caroline County. A docent is on hand for tours. Free to the public. Info: carolinehistory.org or 410-479-2055 and leave a message.
FEDERALSBURGSteam Show, Aug. 1, 2 and 3, opens 10 a.m., Showgrounds on Route 313 between Denton and Federalsburg. Free admission and parking. Daily parade at 5 p.m. Friday and Saturday and 4 p.m. Sunday. Steam engines, antique tractors, gas engines and antique cars. Wheat threshing, shingle sawing, full size sawmill, rock crushing and broom making demonstrations. Live music.
Historical Society Open House, Aug. 9 and Sept. 13, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., Exeter House, 408 Old Denton Rd., Federalsburg. Exeter is one of the oldest remaining structures in southern Caroline County and "has been placed on the National Register of Historic places by the United States Department of the Interior circa 1808." Free admission. Donations accepted.
Monday Bingo, 6 p.m. doors open; 7 p.m. bingo begins., Every Monday. Federalsburg VFW Post 5246, 2630 Veterans Drive. Cash prizes, food available.
Aaron's Place Food Pantry, 4 to 6 p.m., Wednesdays, Community Civic League, 3439 Laurel Grove Road.
GOLDSBOROGiving Grace Food Pantry, Goldsboro VFC, 700 Old Line Road. 7 a.m. until; second Saturdays. Info: 302-270-1948.
GREENSBOROFood pantry, 4 to 7 p.m. Thursday, 7 to 9 a.m. Saturday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Monday. Aaron's Place Pantry at Greensboro Connects, 111 S. Main St., side entrance.
PRESTONPeach Festival, Saturday, Aug. 9, 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., Preston Fire House, 3680 Choptank Rd., Preston. Crafters/Vendors. Fresh peaches. Bake table. Soft crab sandwiches, scrapple sandwiches, burgers, hot dogs. Sponsored by Bethesda Methodist Church in Preston. 410-673-7538 Office@bethesdapreston.faith.
RIDGELYSummerfest, Aug. 15 and 16, downtown Denton. Family-friendly festival featuring regional and local entertainment, strolling performers, bounce houses, artisans, firetruck rides, games, food vendors and more. Info: carolinesummerfest.com.
Martin's House & Barn, First Saturdays thrift store open 8 a.m. to noon. Drive-thru pantry and thrift store hours: 8:30 to 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, Thursday and Friday; 6 to 7:30 p.m. Wednesday.

 August 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Calendar 
 
 348
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Those looking to have an event included in the weekly Caroline County calendar are asked to email details to community@stardem.com.DENTONBingo, 7:30 p.m., Tuesdays, American Legion Post 29, 9238 Legion Road. 5 p.m. doors open, 7:30 p.m. games start. Info:410-479-2708.
Samaritan House Thrift Shop, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Wednesday to Friday; 9 a.m. to noon Saturday. 5th Street behind the post office.
Third Thursdays in Downtown Denton, 5 to 7 p.m., third Thursdays, downtown. Businesses extend their hours and offer specials. Info: DowntownDenton.com.
Aaron's Place Food Pantry, 9:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., Tuesday & Wednesday, 401 Aldersgate Drive.
Paws for Reading, 3:40 to 4:25 p.m., every fourth Thursday, Central Branch library. Children ages 5 to 12 can proactice reading to a trained service dog. One registrant per session. Register: carolib.libcal.com.
Museum of Rural Life, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., every Saturday, 16 N. Second Street. World War I and II, a sharecropper's cabin, new Buffalo Soldier exhibit, among many other artifacts and stories about Caroline County. A docent is on hand for tours. Free to the public. Info: carolinehistory.org or 410-479-2055 and leave a message.
FEDERALSBURGHistorical Society Open House, Sept. 13, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., Exeter House, 408 Old Denton Rd., Federalsburg. Exeter is one of the oldest remaining structures in southern Caroline County and "has been placed on the National Register of Historic places by the United States Department of the Interior circa 1808." Free admission. Donations accepted.
Monday Bingo, 6 p.m. doors open; 7 p.m. bingo begins., Every Monday. Federalsburg VFW Post 5246, 2630 Veterans Drive. Cash prizes, food available.
Aaron's Place Food Pantry, 4 to 6 p.m., Wednesdays, Community Civic League, 3439 Laurel Grove Road.
GOLDSBOROGiving Grace Food Pantry, Goldsboro VFC, 700 Old Line Road. 7 a.m. until; second Saturdays. Info: 302-270-1948.
GREENSBOROFood pantry, 4 to 7 p.m. Thursday, 7 to 9 a.m. Saturday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Monday. Aaron's Place Pantry at Greensboro Connects, 111 S. Main St., side entrance.
RIDGELYMartin's House & Barn, First Saturdays thrift store open 8 a.m. to noon. Drive-thru pantry and thrift store hours: 8:30 to 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, Thursday and Friday; 6 to 7:30 p.m. Wednesday.

Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
EASTON FARMERS MARKET, 8 a.m. to noon, 114 N. Harrison Street, Easton. Open rain or shine. Live music. Info: avalonfoundation.org.

PAWS IN THE POOL, 1 to 4 p.m., 107 Virginia Ave. $10 per dog. $5 if you don't have a pet. $15 day of event. For more information, call 410-228-5578.
YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 1 p.m. Yoga for advanced beginners with Suzie Hurley. $20 per class. $150 for 10 classes. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.

title: Ironman: road closures and expected delays
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Ironman: road closures and expected delays

 September 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 349
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Around 2,000 athletes will come to Cambridge this week to test their abilities in the 2025 Maryland Ironman, set to take place on Saturday, Sept. 20.Residents can expect to see road closures during race day and parking limitations beginning Monday.
Gerry Boyle Park at Great Marsh and Long Wharf Parking and Fountain Circle will be closed from now until Sunday, Sept. 21.
On race day, Somerset Avenue from Hambrooks Avenue to Glasgow Street will be closed from 6:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and delays can be expected on Jenkins Creek Road, Route 343 from Lover's Lane to West Side Bypass, during this time as well.
Saturday, delays can be expected at Glasgow Street and Sandy Hill Road from Somerset Avenue to Hambrooks Avenue from 7 a.m. to 11:30 p.m. High Street from Long Wharf to Poplar Street and Poplar Street from High Street to Gay Street will be closed from 8 a.m. to 12:30 a.m.
Delays can also be expected at the Route 16 and Dailsville Road Intersection from 8:15 a.m. to 5 p.m., Egypt Road at Old Field from 8:30 a.m. to 3 a.m. , the Old Field and Route 335 Intersection from 8:45 a.m. to 3 p.m., and Route 343 and at Westside Bypass Intersection from 11:45 a.m. to 5:15 p.m.
More road closures will be seen at Riverside Drive from Maple Street to Bay View Avenue from 12:15 p.m. to 11:30 p.m., Hambrooks Avenue from Bellevue Avenue to Glasgow Street from 12:15 p.m. to 11:30 p.m., Hambrooks from Glenburn to Choptank avenues from 12:15 p.m. to midnight, and Water Street from Choptank Avenue to High Street from 12:15 p.m. to midnight.
Residents north of Sandy Hill Road, can use Linthicum Drive or Radcliffe Drive to access Sandy Hill/Glasgow. To bypass delays on Sandy Hill/Glasgow, residents can use Jenkins Creek and Holly Terrace. Residents in the Historic District can use Glasgow and Locust to enter or exit town.
According to the Ironman website, police will be monitoring and guiding cars that need to exit or enter the one-way streets off of Hambrooks to the next opposite one-way street during the race.

title: Frederick Douglass Day was a success in Easton
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Frederick Douglass Day was a success in Easton

 September 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Headlines 
 
 98
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Frederick Douglass Day in Easton brought many people together this past weekend.While the forecast showed precipitation, the rain held up long enough for the event to be completed at the courthouse.
It was great to see multiple generations come celebrate Frederick Douglass. Every time I cover something Frederick-Douglass-related, I always learn something new about Douglass.
The Frederick Douglass Honor Society did a great job of combining the younger and older generations for the event, which was something they focused on heavily this year.
You can read more about what I learned by clicking on my story below.
Thanks for reading.
—Ahmad Garnett

 I want to express my appreciation to the Star Democrat for its article in the Oct. 4 paper highlighting the Witch Paddle breast cancer fundraising, fun-raising event I am cosponsoring with several others on Wednesday, Oct. 15, from 4:30-7:30 p.m. at The Oaks Waterfront Hotel in Royal Oak.We look forward to hosting the community — as paddlers, spectators and families. title: Mid-Shore Community Foundation welcomes eight new members
author: SUBMITTED NEWS
content:
Mid-Shore Community Foundation welcomes eight new members

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED NEWS | Section: News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Mid-Shore Community Foundation welcomes eight new members to its board of directors: Leslie Bishop, Suze Chaffinch, LaMonte Cooke, Kathleen Deoudes, Rabbi Peter E. Hyman, Richard "Rich" Loeffler, Margaret "Peggy" Rennels and Arraminta Ware.The Foundation works with donors to establish funds for the region — funds that are distributed as grants and scholarships, provides training programs and endowment management services to area nonprofits, and supports start‐up charities and local charitable projects through fiscal sponsorship.
"As one of the founding board members, I am always pleased to welcome a new slate of directors to this outstanding organization," said Moorhead Vermilye, president of the board of directors. "With Buck Duncan at the helm and a robust, working board of directors, MSCF does exponential good on the Mid-Shore. We love to see more people energized and inspired by the work."
Vermilye said he was grateful for the 2025 board of directors and thanked outgoing board members Bill Christopher, Joe Holt, John Lewis, Becky Loukides, Jenny Rhodes and Tracy Tyler for their service to the Mid-Shore.
In 2016, after raising two sons and having a career as a residential interior designer, Leslie Bishop and her husband retired to Cambridge from Washington, D.C., and soon after, she founded MidShore Meals til Monday, a supplemental food program for children and families facing food insecurity in Dorchester County.
Suze Chaffinch of Denton was born and raised on the Eastern Shore and has lived most of her life in Caroline County. As an elementary school teacher, she taught for many years at Greensboro Elementary School. Since retirement, she has enjoyed volunteering with various organizations. Chaffinch previously served on the Foundation board from 2018 to 2024.
LaMonte Cooke of Chestertown is the director of the Queen Anne's County Department of Corrections, a position he has held since 1987. He has more than 40 years of criminal justice and government service experience, including serving as the first African American Kent County Deputy Sheriff.
Kathleen "Kathy" Deoudes currently serves as chair of the UMMS Shore Regional Health Board of Directors. Before retirement, she worked in the Maryland State Senate as a legislative aide to state Sen. E.J. Pipkin. She lives in Queen Anne's County with her husband Nick. Deoudes served on the Foundation board from 2017 to 2023.
Rabbi Peter E. Hyman of Easton recently retired after serving 18 years as the first full-time rabbi at Easton's Temple B'nai Israel. Hyman is very active in the community, and he has a long history of promoting greater understanding and respect for individuals with different religious beliefs.
Richard "Rich" Loeffler has worked as a business consultant for the Maryland Small Business Development Center (SBDC). Before working for the SBDC, Loeffler was part owner of a small manufacturing company located in Dorchester County, where he served as president of the Dorchester YMCA and on the board of directors for Dorchester General Hospital.
Margaret "Peggy" Rennels was born and raised in Talbot County. After graduating from Easton High School and Skidmore College, she received her M.D. at the University of Maryland School of Medicine. Rennels cared for patients, taught, and was involved with clinical evaluations of vaccines for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Food and Drug Administration. Since retirement, she has devoted her energies to the wellbeing of children through her work on the board of directors of the Critchlow Adkins Children's Center. Rennels served on the Foundation board 2018 to 2024.
Arraminta Ware grew up on a farm near Sudlersville. After graduating from Lynchburg College with an accounting degree, Ware began working in Chestertown, where she is a principal with Anthony, Judge and Ware LLC. Ware lives near Chestertown with her husband Eric Schrader, a self-employed farmer. She serves on the board of directors of Chesapeake Bank and Trust and served on the Foundation board from 2016 to 2022.
Officers for the 2026 board of directors are Vermilye, chair; Alice Ryan, vice chair; Carrie Manuel, treasurer; David Nagel, assistant treasurer and Andy Meehan, secretary.

title: Sons and Daughters of American Revolution hold membership workshop
author: Staff Writer
content:
Sons and Daughters of American Revolution hold membership workshop

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 168
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Oct. 25 from 2-4 p.m., the Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the Maryland Society Sons of the American Revolution and the General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution will sponsor a workshop hosted by the Talbot County Free Library in Easton.The workshop is titled "How to Join the SAR or DAR." Both organizations will have representatives present who will provide a brief overview about the founding and mission of both organizations as well as the activities they provide for members and services they provide to residents of the Mid-Shore community.
Afterward, members of the organizations will help those interested in joining either organization perform online family history research to create a family tree diagram and begin to prepare a membership application that traces an individual's lineage back to one of their patriot ancestors.
The event is free and open to the public. Seating is limited. If interested in participating in this workshop, please reply by sending an email to WesleyOHagood@gmail.com.
Light refreshments will be served.
